The Blackthroat seaperch (Doederleinia berycoides) is a commercially important serranid species inhabiting the continental shelves of the western Pacific, where it supports significant fisheries across Japan, Korea, and China. Recent field surveys have provided detailed life-history data for this species, particularly regarding its reproductive biology. During the spawning season, females extrude pelagic eggs that are notably small, with a mean diameter of approximately 0.75 mm. The corresponding wet weight at birth, determined from volumetric calculations based on this egg dimension, is estimated at 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams]. This remarkably low initial mass is typical of marine teleosts that produce large numbers of small, yolk-poor ova as part of a broadcast spawning strategy. The tiny size of the fertilised ova imposes a brief, energy-limited yolk-sac larval phase before the developing individuals must successfully capture their first planktonic prey to avoid starvation. Field-based growth studies indicate that maximum adult body mass is attained around one kilogram [Wwi = around one kilogram], placing this species among the moderately large-bodied members of its family, with some trophy specimens reportedly reaching even higher weights in deeper, less exploited waters.

Puberty in Doederleinia berycoides is reached at a total length of 27.2 centimeters [Lp = 27.2 centimeters], marking the onset of gonadal differentiation and the beginning of reproductive capacity. This length at the initiation of sexual maturation is a critical demographic parameter used by fisheries managers to establish minimum size limits for harvest, ensuring that individuals have the opportunity to spawn at least once before entering the fishery. The transition from a juvenile to a reproductively mature state involves significant physiological changes, including the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, which drives vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. Comparative data suggest that this length at puberty is relatively high for a serranid of its asymptotic size, potentially reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritises somatic growth and competitive ability on the reef before energy is diverted toward gamete production. Individuals shorter than this threshold are considered immature and do not contribute to the breeding population, making the preservation of adult size classes essential for population sustainability. Seasonal cycles in water temperature and photoperiod are thought to synchronise the precise timing of gonadal recrudescence.

The ultimate total length attained by this species has been documented at 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], representing the maximum size an individual can achieve under favourable environmental conditions. This asymptotic length is a key descriptor of the species growth trajectory and is frequently employed in stock assessment models to estimate biomass and fishing mortality rates. Growth in the Blackthroat seaperch follows a decelerating pattern common to many demersal fishes, with rapid length increases during the first few years of life followed by a gradual plateau as metabolic resources are increasingly redirected toward maintenance and reproduction. Mark-recapture studies conducted in the East China Sea have confirmed that individuals approach this upper size limit slowly, indicating a relatively long-lived species that invests in sustained growth over many years. The measurements obtained from otolith-based age readings corroborate the growth model, showing that the largest specimens are also among the oldest in the population. This ultimate length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters] is used as a reference point for comparing growth performance across related serranid species.

Longevity records for Doederleinia berycoides indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately ten years [am = approximately ten years] when maintained under average oceanic temperatures of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a thermal regime characteristic of its preferred depth range on the continental shelf. This lifespan estimate, derived from otolith annulus counts in wild-caught individuals, places the Blackthroat seaperch as a moderately long-lived teleost among the temperate serranids. The correlation between low ambient temperature and extended lifespan is well documented in fish, and the 15 °C [T = 15 °C] isotherm appears to delineate the optimal thermal window for slow ageing and high survival in this species. Individuals residing in warmer, shallower waters may experience accelerated metabolic rates and consequently shorter maximum ages, while those in deeper, cooler habitats may live longer. Understanding the thermal dependency of senescence is crucial for predicting population responses to climate-driven ocean warming, as elevated temperatures could reduce the average generation time. The maximum recorded lifespan of ten years [am = ten years] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] thus serves as a baseline for evaluating the species vulnerability to environmental change.

Reproductive output in the Blackthroat seaperch is characterised by high fecundity and iteroparous spawning across multiple seasons. Mature females produce a large number of small pelagic eggs during each spawning event, with annual reproductive effort reflecting a balance between current fecundity and future survival. The total length at puberty of 27.2 centimeters [Lp = 27.2 centimeters] ensures that only individuals that have achieved substantial growth are recruited into the spawning population, thereby linking body size directly to lifetime reproductive success. Given the small egg mass of 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams], the energetic cost of individual ova is minimal, allowing females to allocate a significant proportion of their annual energy budget toward producing thousands of offspring per season. The ultimate body mass of approximately one kilogram [Wwi = approximately one kilogram] further constrains the total number of eggs that can be carried at any one time, as abdominal cavity volume limits the maximum gonadal mass. This combination of moderate adult size, late maturation, and prodigious egg output defines a life-history strategy that is sensitive to overfishing, as the removal of large, fecund individuals can rapidly deplete the reproductive potential of the population.
